judge.verdict: The city survived the full twenty years with no default, depopulation, or revolt, and housing stayed impressively well-matched to population (ratio 1.02-1.12) throughout, while happiness trended upward from the high-60s to the high-80s. Pollution also crept upward overall (26.9 to 28.5, peaking near 30.5) rather than being reversed. The single most consequential choice was the shift after year 11-12 away from business subsidies/factory construction and toward pure tax-and-hoard governance, which set the jobs-to-population ratio on an eight-year downward slide that the terminal happiness numbers do not redeem.

The main blemish is fiscal: debt sat frozen at 2200 for all twenty years with no repayment even as treasury surplus swelled to over 3000, suggesting under-optimized capital management rather than any acute risk.

judge.verdict: The city never escaped the debt hole it dug in year 1, when it borrowed 4000 in debt and immediately spent it on subsidies while holding tax rate at a middling 0.3%—treasury started at -694 and never once turned upward, falling in a near-monotonic slide to -3097 by year 12 even as jobs and services fluctuated; that initial over-leveraging without a repayment or revenue-growth plan made the eventual bankruptcy structurally inevitable rather than a sudden shock, and the year-12 happiness collapse to 25.1 was merely the visible endpoint of a fiscal trajectory that was unrecoverable from year 1 onward.
